category.name: Active Directory
category.description: Incidents in on-premises Active Directory: Kerberos abuse, credential theft from DCs, privilege escalation, persistence, delegation abuse, and Tier 0 compromise.

playbooks.name: Kerberoasting: bulk RC4 service ticket requests from one account
playbooks.summary: Use when a single user or host requests many TGS tickets for SPN-bearing accounts, often with RC4 encryption, suggesting offline cracking of service account passwords.

preparation: Enable Audit Kerberos Service Ticket Operations on all domain controllers so 4769 is logged
Maintain an inventory of user accounts with SPNs and their owners
Deploy a honey SPN account with no legitimate use to alert on any ticket request
Enforce AES-only encryption types on service accounts where applications support it
identification: Search 4769 events for TicketEncryptionType 0x17 grouped by requesting account and source IP
Count distinct ServiceName values requested by the suspect account in a 10-minute window
Identify the process on the source host that issued the requests via Sysmon or EDR telemetry
List which requested SPN accounts are privileged or have weak, old passwords
containment: Disable or reset the password of the account that issued the bulk TGS requests
Isolate the source workstation in EDR pending forensic review
Rotate passwords on every privileged SPN account whose ticket was requested, using 25+ characters
eradication: Remove the roasting tool and any staged hash output files from the source host
Convert eligible service accounts to gMSA so passwords rotate automatically
Remove unused SPNs and strip SPNs from accounts in privileged groups
recovery: Restart dependent services after service account password rotation and confirm they authenticate
Monitor 4624 logons by the rotated service accounts for use from unexpected hosts for 30 days
Re-enable the requesting user only after a credential reset and device rebuild
lessons: Add a detection for one account requesting more than N distinct SPN tickets in a short window
Track the count of RC4-capable service accounts as a hardening metric
Review why privileged service accounts had crackable passwords and set a rotation policy

splunk.title: RC4 TGS requests by account and source
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4769 Ticket_Encryption_Type=0x17 Service_Name!="*$" | stats dc(Service_Name) as spns values(Service_Name) as services by Account_Name, Client_Address | where spns > 5 | sort - spns

splunk.title: Honey SPN ticket requests
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4769 Service_Name="<honey_spn_account>" | table _time, Account_Name, Client_Address, Ticket_Encryption_Type

splunk.title: Logons by rotated service accounts after reset
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.user IN (<svc_account_list>) by Authentication.user, Authentication.src, Authentication.dest | rename Authentication.* as *

playbooks.name: AS-REP roasting of accounts without Kerberos pre-authentication
playbooks.summary: Use when AS-REQ traffic targets accounts flagged DONT_REQ_PREAUTH, letting an attacker collect encrypted AS-REP data to crack offline without any credentials.

preparation: Audit Kerberos Authentication Service on DCs so 4768 events include pre-auth type
Report weekly on accounts with userAccountControl DONT_REQ_PREAUTH set
Document the business owner for every account that legitimately needs pre-auth disabled
identification: Search 4768 events with PreAuthType 0 to list targeted accounts and requesting IPs
Query AD for all accounts where userAccountControl includes 4194304
Check whether the requesting IP is a domain-joined host or an unmanaged device
Determine whether any roastable account has privileged group membership
containment: Enable Kerberos pre-authentication on every targeted account that does not strictly need it
Reset passwords on roastable accounts that were targeted
Block the unmanaged source IP at the network edge or NAC
eradication: Locate and remove the tooling used to send AS-REQ requests from the source host
Replace legacy apps requiring disabled pre-auth with supported authentication
Remove stale accounts that were found with pre-auth disabled
recovery: Confirm targeted accounts authenticate normally with pre-auth enabled
Watch for 4768 PreAuthType 0 events recurring against the same accounts
Verify no successful logon used the targeted accounts from new sources
lessons: Add a scheduled check that alerts when DONT_REQ_PREAUTH is set on any account
Alert on AS-REQ without pre-auth from non-server subnets
Record how long roastable accounts existed before discovery

splunk.title: AS-REQ without pre-authentication
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4768 Pre_Authentication_Type=0 | stats count values(Account_Name) as targets by Client_Address | sort - count

splunk.title: UAC changes that disable pre-auth
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4738 "Don't Require Preauth" | table _time, Subject_Account_Name, Target_Account_Name, New_UAC_Value

playbooks.name: DCSync: directory replication requested by a non-DC account
playbooks.summary: Use when a user or host that is not a domain controller invokes DRSUAPI GetNCChanges replication rights, typically to dump krbtgt and admin password hashes.

preparation: Enable Audit Directory Service Access with SACLs on the domain root for replication GUIDs
Keep an allowlist of DC computer accounts and Entra Connect accounts holding replication rights
Capture DRSUAPI traffic metadata from DC network sensors or NDR
identification: Search 4662 events for replication GUIDs 1131f6aa and 1131f6ad from non-DC accounts
Identify the source IP of the replication request and map it to a host
Review the domain root ACL for unexpected Replicating Directory Changes All grants
Determine which account hashes were likely retrieved, assuming krbtgt is included
containment: Disable the account that performed replication and isolate the source host
Remove any non-standard replication rights from the domain root ACL
Start the double krbtgt reset procedure if krbtgt exposure is likely
Reset passwords for all Tier 0 accounts whose hashes were replicated
eradication: Hunt for persistence the attacker added with the stolen hashes such as new admins or GPOs
Remove dumping tools and output files from the source host
Rebuild the source host from a known good image
recovery: Complete the second krbtgt reset after replication convergence
Monitor 4662 replication events for any recurrence from non-DC sources
Confirm Entra Connect and other legitimate sync still function after ACL cleanup
lessons: Deploy a standing alert for replication GUID access by non-DC principals
Review how the attacker gained an account with replication rights
Add replication right holders to the quarterly Tier 0 access review

splunk.title: Replication rights used by non-DC accounts
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4662 (Properties="*1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2*" OR Properties="*1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2*") Account_Name!="*$" | stats count by Account_Name, Object_Name, ComputerName

splunk.title: Network logons on DCs from the replication source
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=3 Source_Network_Address="<ioc_ip>" host IN (<dc_list>) | table _time, host, Account_Name, Authentication_Package

splunk.title: Domain root ACL changes
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name=nTSecurityDescriptor DN="DC=*" | table _time, Subject_Account_Name, DN, Attribute_Value

playbooks.name: Golden Ticket: forged TGTs signed with a stolen krbtgt key
playbooks.summary: Use when Kerberos activity shows TGTs that no DC issued, abnormal ticket lifetimes, or nonexistent users, indicating the krbtgt hash is compromised.

preparation: Record krbtgt password last set date and rotate it at least twice a year
Retain 4768 and 4769 events from all DCs for at least 90 days
Pre-stage the Microsoft krbtgt reset script and test it in a lab forest
identification: Find 4769 service ticket requests with no matching 4768 TGT issuance for that account and host
Look for Kerberos logons by usernames that do not exist in AD
Check for ticket lifetimes exceeding the domain policy maximum in EDR Kerberos telemetry
Trace how the krbtgt hash was exposed via DCSync, NTDS theft, or DC compromise
containment: Reset krbtgt once, wait for replication, then reset it again to invalidate forged TGTs
Isolate hosts where forged tickets were used
Restrict Tier 0 logon to PAWs while the reset is underway
eradication: Close the original access path that yielded the krbtgt key
Hunt for additional persistence: new admin accounts, SID history, AdminSDHolder changes
Rebuild any DC that was directly compromised
recovery: Verify Kerberos authentication health on all DCs after both resets
Monitor for 4769 events with failure codes indicating old forged tickets being replayed
Confirm trusts and cross-forest authentication still function
lessons: Add correlation detection for TGS requests lacking a preceding TGT
Shorten the krbtgt rotation interval and automate it
Measure time between krbtgt exposure and reset completion

splunk.title: TGS without preceding TGT for the account
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode IN (4768,4769) | eval acct=lower(mvindex(split(Account_Name,"@"),0)) | stats values(EventCode) as codes by acct, Client_Address | where mvcount(codes)=1 AND codes=4769

splunk.title: Kerberos logons by nonexistent users
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4624 Authentication_Package=Kerberos | lookup ad_users sAMAccountName as Account_Name OUTPUT sAMAccountName as known | where isnull(known) AND NOT match(Account_Name,"\$$") | stats count by Account_Name, host

playbooks.name: Silver Ticket: forged service tickets for a single server
playbooks.summary: Use when a server accepts Kerberos service tickets that no DC issued, implying the attacker holds that computer or service account's key and forges TGS locally.

preparation: Enable PAC validation where supported on high-value servers
Forward 4624 and 4634 logon events from Tier 0 and Tier 1 servers to the SIEM
Ensure computer account password rotation is not disabled by GPO
identification: Find 4624 Kerberos logons on the target server with no 4769 for that SPN on any DC
Identify which service class is abused such as CIFS, HOST, MSSQLSvc, or HTTP
Check whether the server's machine account hash was dumped via LSASS or registry
Review logon account names and group SIDs for impossible combinations
containment: Reset the target computer account password twice with Reset-ComputerMachinePassword
Reset the service account password if a user-based SPN was forged
Restrict network access to the affected server to admin jump hosts
eradication: Remove credential dumping artifacts from the server
Hunt for scheduled tasks or services created during forged sessions
Patch or harden the server path used to extract the machine key
recovery: Confirm the server's secure channel with Test-ComputerSecureChannel
Watch for further DC-less Kerberos logons on the server for 14 days
Return network access after secure channel and EDR scans are clean
lessons: Build a detection joining server 4624 Kerberos logons to DC 4769 events
Review where machine account rotation was disabled
Add service accounts with forged tickets to the gMSA migration list

splunk.title: Server Kerberos logons without DC ticket issuance
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4624 Authentication_Package=Kerberos host="<host>" | stats earliest(_time) as first by Account_Name, Source_Network_Address | join type=left Account_Name [search index=wineventlog EventCode=4769 Service_Name="<host>$" | stats count as tgs by Account_Name] | where isnull(tgs)

splunk.title: Machine account password resets
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4742 Target_Account_Name="<host>$" | table _time, Subject_Account_Name, Target_Account_Name, Password_Last_Set

playbooks.name: NTDS.dit copied from a domain controller
playbooks.summary: Use when a DC shows ntdsutil IFM creation, Volume Shadow Copy access to NTDS.dit, or SYSTEM hive export, meaning every domain password hash may be in attacker hands.

preparation: Enable process creation logging with command line on all domain controllers
Alert on vssadmin, ntdsutil, and diskshadow execution on DCs
Restrict interactive logon on DCs to a small named Tier 0 group
Keep offline, tested system-state backups of at least two DCs
identification: Search DC process logs for ntdsutil "ac i ntds" ifm or vssadmin create shadow
Look for copies of ntds.dit or SYSTEM hive in temp, share, or web folders on the DC
Trace outbound SMB, HTTP, or cloud storage transfers from the DC around the copy time
Identify the account and logon session that ran the extraction commands
containment: Isolate the DC from non-DC networks while keeping replication with peers
Disable the account that executed the extraction and kill its sessions
Delete shadow copies and staged ntds.dit or hive copies after evidence capture
Begin a domain-wide password reset plan prioritizing Tier 0 and service accounts
eradication: Perform the double krbtgt reset
Reset all privileged, service, and trust account passwords
Force a password change at next logon for all users
Rebuild the affected DC from media rather than cleaning it in place
recovery: Monitor for pass-the-hash use of pre-reset hashes across the estate
Confirm all trust passwords were rotated and trusts validate
Track completion percentage of the domain-wide password reset daily
lessons: Add detection for IFM creation and NTDS.dit file reads by non-system processes
Review how the attacker gained interactive access to a DC
Measure the time from extraction to full credential rotation

splunk.title: NTDS extraction commands on DCs
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.dest IN (<dc_list>) (Processes.process="*ntdsutil*ifm*" OR Processes.process="*vssadmin*create shadow*" OR Processes.process="*ntds.dit*" OR Processes.process="*reg* save*hklm\\system*") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process | rename Processes.* as *

splunk.title: Large outbound transfers from DCs
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.src IN (<dc_ip_list>) by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port | where bytes > 50000000 | rename All_Traffic.* as *

splunk.title: File creation of ntds.dit copies
splunk.spl: index=sysmon sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=11 TargetFilename="*ntds.dit" NOT TargetFilename="C:\\Windows\\NTDS\\*" | table _time, host, Image, TargetFilename

playbooks.name: Password spray against domain controllers
playbooks.summary: Use when one source tries a few common passwords against many domain accounts via Kerberos or NTLM, staying under lockout thresholds to find weak credentials.

preparation: Collect 4771 and 4776 failures from every DC, not just the PDC emulator
Deploy a banned password list through Entra Password Protection or a filter DLL
Know the domain lockout threshold and observation window values
identification: Group 4771 code 0x18 and 4776 0xC000006A failures by source and count distinct targeted users
Find accounts with a success from the spraying source after failures
Map the spraying source IP to a host, VPN user, or exposed service
Check whether the spray targeted only enabled users, indicating prior enumeration
containment: Block the spraying source IP at the firewall or VPN concentrator
Force password resets for accounts that authenticated successfully during the spray
Revoke VPN and remote access sessions of compromised accounts
eradication: Remove malware or tooling on the internal host that sourced the spray
Expire passwords that match the sprayed seasonal patterns
Close any internet-facing service that exposed NTLM authentication
recovery: Monitor compromised accounts for logons from new hosts for two weeks
Confirm the spraying source no longer generates authentication failures
Notify affected users and verify their new passwords meet policy
lessons: Tune a detection for one source failing against more than 20 distinct accounts
Report how many accounts used a sprayed password
Evaluate smart lockout or MFA for internal-facing remote access

splunk.title: Spray pattern: one source, many users
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=4771 Failure_Code=0x18) OR (EventCode=4776 Error_Code=0xC000006A) | eval src=coalesce(Client_Address, Source_Workstation) | bin _time span=30m | stats dc(Account_Name) as users count by _time, src | where users > 20

splunk.title: Successful logons from the spray source
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.src="<ioc_ip>" Authentication.action=success by Authentication.user, Authentication.dest | rename Authentication.* as *

playbooks.name: Account lockout storm across the domain
playbooks.summary: Use when hundreds of accounts lock out in a short window from brute force or a misconfigured device, disrupting logons and possibly masking an attack.

preparation: Forward 4740 lockout events with Caller Computer Name from the PDC emulator
Pre-approve a bulk unlock script and the authority to run it
Document how to identify service accounts and mapped drives using stale credentials
identification: Count 4740 events per minute and list the top Caller Computer Name values
Distinguish attack from misconfiguration by checking whether one source hits many users
Inspect the caller host for services, scheduled tasks, or apps with saved bad credentials
Check whether locked accounts include help desk or emergency admins
containment: Block or quarantine the caller host generating the bad authentications
Temporarily raise the lockout threshold under change control if the storm is ongoing
Prioritize unlocking accounts needed for incident response and critical operations
eradication: Correct the stored credential on misconfigured devices or services
Remove the brute-force tool or malware if the source is attacker-controlled
Disable legacy protocols on the source system that retry with cached passwords
recovery: Bulk unlock affected accounts once the source is stopped
Restore the original lockout policy and confirm GPO application
Watch the 4740 rate for 24 hours to confirm it returns to baseline
lessons: Alert when lockouts exceed baseline by a set multiple in 15 minutes
Review whether lockout policy itself is a denial-of-service risk
Record root cause: attack, stale credential, or tooling error

splunk.title: Lockouts per minute by caller computer
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4740 | bin _time span=1m | stats dc(Target_Account_Name) as accounts by _time, Caller_Computer_Name | sort - accounts

splunk.title: Failure sources for locked accounts
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode IN (4625,4771,4776) Account_Name IN (<locked_accounts>) | eval src=coalesce(Source_Network_Address, Client_Address, Source_Workstation) | stats count by src, Account_Name | sort - count

playbooks.name: Unexpected account added to Domain Admins
playbooks.summary: Use when an account is added to Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins, or Administrators without a matching change ticket.

preparation: Alert on 4728, 4732, and 4756 events for all built-in privileged groups
Keep an approved baseline of privileged group membership
Require change tickets for any Tier 0 group modification
identification: Identify who added the member, from which DC, and the source logon session
Confirm with the change owner whether a ticket exists for the addition
Review activity of the newly added account since the addition time
Check whether the adder account itself was recently compromised or elevated
containment: Remove the unauthorized member from the privileged group
Disable the added account and the account that performed the change
Purge Kerberos tickets of the added account on hosts it touched with klist purge
eradication: Review all actions the added admin took, including GPO, ACL, and account changes
Revert persistence created with the elevated account
Reset passwords for the actor and any credentials the admin could have harvested
recovery: Compare current privileged group membership against the approved baseline
Re-enable legitimate accounts after credential reset and review
Monitor privileged groups at increased sensitivity for 30 days
lessons: Evaluate just-in-time privileged access to shrink standing Domain Admin membership
Measure time from group change to alert triage
Review whether delegated OU admins could modify Tier 0 groups

splunk.title: Privileged group membership additions
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode IN (4728,4732,4756) Group_Name IN ("Domain Admins","Enterprise Admins","Schema Admins","Administrators") | table _time, host, Subject_Account_Name, Member_Name, Group_Name

splunk.title: Activity of the new admin account
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" Account_Name="<suspect_user>" earliest=<added_time> | stats count values(EventCode) as events by host

splunk.title: Change data model view of the group change
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.object_category=group All_Changes.object IN ("Domain Admins","Enterprise Admins") by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.object, All_Changes.action | rename All_Changes.* as *

playbooks.name: AdminSDHolder ACL tampered for persistence
playbooks.summary: Use when the AdminSDHolder object's security descriptor gains a new ACE, which SDProp then stamps onto every protected admin account and group every hour.

preparation: Set a SACL on CN=AdminSDHolder,CN=System to audit writes to nTSecurityDescriptor
Export and store a baseline of the AdminSDHolder ACL
Know the SDProp interval and how to trigger it manually
identification: Search 5136 events on CN=AdminSDHolder for nTSecurityDescriptor changes
Diff the current AdminSDHolder ACL against the stored baseline
Identify the trustee granted rights and what rights such as GenericAll or WriteDACL
Check protected accounts with adminCount=1 for the propagated ACE
containment: Remove the rogue ACE from AdminSDHolder
Disable the trustee account or remove it from the group granted the ACE
Run SDProp manually via RunProtectAdminGroupsTask to repropagate the clean ACL
eradication: Verify the rogue ACE is gone from every protected object after SDProp
Review what the trustee did with its rights such as password resets or group changes
Reset credentials of any protected account the trustee could have controlled
recovery: Re-export the AdminSDHolder ACL and confirm it matches baseline
Monitor 4724 password resets and 4728 group adds by the former trustee
Confirm legitimate delegated tooling still works with the restored ACL
lessons: Add an hourly diff job of the AdminSDHolder ACL
Review who holds rights to modify objects under CN=System
Include AdminSDHolder checks in Tier 0 audits

splunk.title: Writes to AdminSDHolder security descriptor
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 DN="CN=AdminSDHolder,CN=System,*" Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name=nTSecurityDescriptor | table _time, host, Subject_Account_Name, Operation_Type, Attribute_Value

splunk.title: Password resets on protected accounts
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4724 Subject_Account_Name="<suspect_user>" | table _time, Subject_Account_Name, Target_Account_Name, host

playbooks.name: Group Policy Object modified to deploy attacker persistence
playbooks.summary: Use when a GPO linked to many computers gains a new scheduled task, startup script, or registry change that runs attacker code across the domain.

preparation: Audit writes to groupPolicyContainer objects and SYSVOL Policies folders
Back up all GPOs nightly with Backup-GPO and keep versions offline
Restrict GPO edit rights to a named Group Policy admin group
identification: Search 5136 events on groupPolicyContainer objects for versionNumber and gPCMachineExtensionNames changes
Inspect SYSVOL for new ScheduledTasks.xml, scripts.ini, or Registry.pol files in the GPO GUID folder
Compare the modified GPO against last night's backup with a GPO report diff
List OUs the GPO is linked to and estimate how many hosts already applied it
containment: Unlink or disable the modified GPO immediately
Remove edit permissions from the account that made the change
Block the payload hash and C2 domains referenced by the GPO task in EDR and proxy
eradication: Restore the GPO from the known good backup
Delete scheduled tasks or services the GPO created on every endpoint via EDR
Remove payload files dropped from SYSVOL or network shares
recovery: Run gpupdate /force on affected OUs and confirm the clean version number applies
Hunt endpoints for continued execution of the payload for 7 days
Re-link the restored GPO after validation
lessons: Add detection for scheduled task creation via Group Policy client service
Review GPO delegation and remove unnecessary editors
Track how many endpoints executed the malicious GPO before unlink

splunk.title: GPO attribute changes
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 Object_Class=groupPolicyContainer | table _time, Subject_Account_Name, DN, Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name, Attribute_Value

splunk.title: Scheduled tasks created by Group Policy
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4698 | search Task_Content="*<payload_name>*" | stats count by host, Task_Name

splunk.title: SYSVOL file writes
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5145 Share_Name="*SYSVOL" Relative_Target_Name="*Policies*" Accesses="*WriteData*" | table _time, Account_Name, Source_Address, Relative_Target_Name

playbooks.name: Bulk LAPS local admin password reads
playbooks.summary: Use when an account reads ms-Mcs-AdmPwd or msLAPS-Password attributes for many computers, giving it local admin on each and a lateral movement path.

preparation: Configure SACLs to audit read access to LAPS password attributes
Document which groups are delegated LAPS read rights per OU
Enable Windows LAPS password expiration after use where available
identification: Search 4662 events for reads of the LAPS password attribute GUID by account
Count distinct computers whose LAPS password the suspect account read
Check for 4624 logon type 3 with local admin accounts on those computers afterwards
Review who granted the suspect account LAPS read rights
containment: Remove the suspect account from groups with LAPS read delegation
Force LAPS password rotation on every computer that was read
Disable the suspect account pending review
eradication: Hunt read computers for tools, services, or users added using local admin
Remove excess LAPS read ACEs found with Find-AdmPwdExtendedRights
Rotate credentials cached on hosts accessed with local admin
recovery: Confirm new LAPS passwords were written and expiration times reset
Monitor local administrator logons across the read computers
Restore least-privilege LAPS delegation to helpdesk tiers
lessons: Alert when one account reads more than 10 LAPS passwords in an hour
Include LAPS read delegation in quarterly access reviews
Assess moving to Windows LAPS with encrypted passwords and history

splunk.title: LAPS attribute reads by account
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4662 (Properties="*ms-Mcs-AdmPwd*" OR Properties="*msLAPS-Password*" OR Properties="*<laps_attr_guid>*") | stats dc(Object_Name) as computers values(Object_Name) as objs by Account_Name | sort - computers

splunk.title: Local admin network logons after reads
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=3 Account_Name="Administrator" Account_Domain!="<domain>" host IN (<read_computers>) | table _time, host, Source_Network_Address

playbooks.name: AD CS abuse: ESC1 template misuse or ESC8 relay to web enrollment
playbooks.summary: Use when a certificate is issued with an arbitrary SAN for a privileged user, or NTLM is relayed to the CA's HTTP enrollment endpoint to obtain a DC certificate.

preparation: Enable CA auditing for certificate requests and issuance events 4886 and 4887
Inventory templates with ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT and client authentication EKU
Require EPA and HTTPS or disable the certsrv web enrollment role
Know how to revoke certificates and publish an updated CRL quickly
identification: Search 4887 events for certificates whose SAN differs from the requester
Find certificate requests for DC or admin subjects from a non-admin requester
Check IIS logs on the CA for NTLM authentication to /certsrv from DC machine accounts
Look for 4768 PKINIT logons using the newly issued certificate
containment: Revoke the maliciously issued certificates and publish the CRL
Disable the vulnerable template or remove the supply-in-request flag
Stop the CA web enrollment endpoint or enforce EPA
Reset credentials of the impersonated account and purge its tickets
eradication: Add the revoked certificate thumbprints to NTAuth monitoring and block PKINIT use
Restrict template enrollment rights to specific groups
Hunt for DCSync or admin activity performed with the forged identity
recovery: Re-enable needed templates with manager approval required
Monitor 4887 for SAN mismatches for 30 days
Confirm legitimate enrollment workflows still issue certificates
lessons: Run a recurring AD CS misconfiguration scan and track ESC findings
Add a detection for PKINIT logons by privileged accounts from new hosts
Document the CA as Tier 0 and enforce Tier 0 admin controls on it

splunk.title: Issued certificates with mismatched requester and SAN
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4887 host="<ca_host>" | rex field=Attributes "(?i)san:upn=(?<san_upn>[^&\s]+)" | where isnotnull(san_upn) AND lower(san_upn)!=lower(Requester) | table _time, Requester, san_upn, Template, Request_ID

splunk.title: NTLM auth to CA web enrollment
splunk.spl: index=iis host="<ca_host>" cs_uri_stem="/certsrv*" | stats count by c_ip, cs_username, cs_uri_stem, sc_status

splunk.title: PKINIT logons for privileged users
splunk.spl: index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4768 Pre_Authentication_Type=16 Account_Name IN (<privileged_accounts>) | table _time, Account_Name, Client_Address, Certificate_Thumbprint

playbooks.name: NTLM relay attack against SMB or LDAP services
playbooks.summary: Use when coerced or poisoned NTLM authentication is relayed to another server, often seen as a machine or user authenticating from an IP that is not its own.

preparation: Enforce SMB signing on all servers and LDAP signing and channel binding on DCs
Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS through GPO
Log 4624 events with source IP and NTLM package details on servers
identification: Find NTLM logons where the source IP does not match the account's own host IP
Look for coercion RPC calls such as EfsRpcOpenFileRaw or SpoolSample against DCs
Identify the relay host running responder or ntlmrelayx-style listeners
Review LDAP changes made by the relayed identity such as RBCD or new computer objects
containment: Isolate the relay host
Block inbound SMB and HTTP from the relay host to servers
Revert directory changes the relayed session made
eradication: Remove listener tooling from the relay host
Patch or disable the coerced service such as Print Spooler on DCs
Reset passwords of relayed user accounts
recovery: Validate SMB signing and LDAP channel binding enforcement with a scan
Monitor for NTLM logon source mismatches over two weeks
Confirm that legacy apps work with signing enforcement
lessons: Track the percentage of NTLM authentication versus Kerberos in the domain
Add detection for coercion RPC calls to DCs
Plan NTLM deprecation for remaining dependent systems

playbooks.name: Rogue or unexpected domain controller joining replication
playbooks.summary: Use when an unrecognized domain controller appears in the topology or replicates with legitimate DCs, suggesting an attacker promoted a DC or restored one from media.

preparation: Maintain an authoritative inventory of all legitimate domain controllers
Alert on DC promotion events and new entries in the Domain Controllers OU
Restrict the right to add computers to the domain and to promote DCs
identification: List all DCs with nltest /dclist and compare against the authoritative inventory
Review 4928 and 4929 replication source and destination events for unknown partners
Check the Domain Controllers OU for a computer object you do not recognize
Trace when and by whom the rogue DC was promoted via directory service logs
containment: Network-isolate the rogue DC from the other DCs
Stop inbound and outbound replication with the rogue DC
Disable the account that performed the promotion
eradication: Force demote or metadata-cleanup the rogue DC from the topology
Remove its computer and server objects and DNS records
Run the double krbtgt reset since a rogue DC implies full directory access
recovery: Verify the DC list matches the authoritative inventory
Confirm replication is healthy among legitimate DCs only
Monitor for new DC promotions for 30 days
lessons: Alert on any DC promotion and reconcile against the inventory
Review who holds rights to promote domain controllers
Assess physical and virtual controls preventing rogue DC creation
